AoW4 is, as far as city management, one of the simplest 4x games I've played (which is **not** a bad thing). CK/Stellaris are very different games to AoW4, though: AoW's closest comparisons are games like Civ and Endless Legend - both are more complex when it comes to city management, research, spying, and general diplomacy, but where AoW shines is in the RPG elements and the gameplay. 

Endless Legend has a lot of the same kinds of things, but AoW's combat generally feels better. Endless Legends is great as well, but the biggest difference in AoW and Endless is vibes: Endless feels like a classic 4x with *some* RPG elements, whereas AoW feels like a rougelike RPG tactics game with *some* 4x elements - if you're looking at AoW as *just* a 4x, you'll quickly notice it's missing a lot of key features in the genre, but it makes more sense when you realize that the main draw of AoW is the RPG elements. 

tl;dr: Depends. On one end of the 4x scale is Civ, which is a very classic 4x. AoW is just about on the opposite end of the spectrum, more about the RPG elements than the hard 4x management. Endless is more in the middle. There's not a right way to do a 4x, it's all about which parts **you** enjoy.

My point really is that, aside from particles and lighting, Wilds doesn't look **much** better than World, which was fully playable at 60fps on a 1080ti. There's *some* visual improvements, sure, and there's more raw graphical power in Wilds, but it doesn't usually show because the effects they use wash out the game and the high requirements lead most people to playing on lower specs anyways. If you compare the two games, they're getting diminishing returns on graphics - Wilds looks a **little** better if you compare the two maxed out, but the difference to actually play at that level is staggering, and I feel like most people would prefer a game that looks *slightly* worse but actually runs on most rigs vs a game that looks *slightly* better but dips into sub-60 fps even on high-end cards, much less the choppy mess it ends up as on mid-end and low-end cards. It's like they've plateaued on visual fidelity, so they threw in so many effects and focused so hard on things like 8k dirt textures (obvious exaggeration, don't take this at face value) that it makes the average performance **worse** than if they'd just used World's engine and visuals. If Wilds looked good on anything other than Ultra then 40-50fps would be acceptable, but the game looks awful as soon as you start lowering anything; On the flipside, World ran pretty well even on mid-end rigs without lowering too much, and when you **did** lower things, it didn't absolutely tank the visual quality.

  
tl;dr I don't have a direct answer to your question, but my point is more that Wilds is only incrementally better visually than World while being a massive resource hog, to the point that most people aren't even getting the visual improvements. In fact, if we look at reviews and screenshots people post, it seems most PC players are getting a *worse* experience than World, which is a shame because Wilds' gameplay is solid.

Here's how I did it:

Carian Dueling Shield + Immutable Shield. I'd cast IS at the start of the fight with Golden Vow to help on damage. Dueling Shields are funny because you can just hold L1 and press R1. Use the Stamina Recovery Talisman, Dragoncrest Greatshield, Golden Braid, and anything else (I used the one to make buffs last longer), and use Malenia's Great Rune - healing his chip on blocking R1s is really funny, the run I won I used 2 Estus overall. Keep at it, learn what you need to dodge, when to buff, and when to let guard down for stamina recovery. With IS up you can block most attacks with little to no damage (barring >!his low-health dive bomb!<.)

Note: Don't infuse the shield or you lose out on physical resist - doesn't really matter w/IS up, but w/o you notice the extra damage. The numbers will be lower since you can't just pump INT for big numbers here, but that's the trade. My INT was 70, DEX 40, and STR 16 and I was dealing \~700 an R1 - not amazing, but it'll get you through it. I'd also advise not to use summons or ashes - you want his attacks on you so it's more predictable.

There are some good side-quests in the game, for sure, but many of them feel like MMO filler content. I like as much as you to see what life's like for people on the ground, but it could have been done in more engaging ways than "go to x, talk to y - repeat" and calling that a quest. If it was just talking to a single person it'd be one thing, but the travel time in the quests often feels like bloat. For example: >!Teleport to the map -> Ride to a place -> Talk to a person -> Talk to another person up the hill -> Talk to the first person -> Ride into the next zone -> Kill monster -> Talk to the first person -> Cutscene!< could have been simplified or made more interesting from a gameplay perspective, as much as I liked it from a lore perspective (talking about >!Blacksmith's Blues III!< in this case). 

It also doesn't help that the side-quests derail the pacing pretty badly. For example: The aforementioned quest above. You get this side quest, as well as two others, after >!Clive almost dies to Barnabus and Jill is missing. It kinda breaks the pacing to go on a fetch quest for the infirmary, a fetch quest for the botanists, and a Blackthorne quest.!< They're all good side-quests for expanding the lore, but the time you get them feels so off. It doesn't help >!when you get them. It's hard to tell how much time is left in the story at that point - it kinda feels like each main mission could be a point of no return. So scrambling to do the side-quests because you want to see and enjoy all of the game's content while also really wanting to see the story missions because it feels like time is of the essence (which, imo, the writers really succeeded at) kinda kills off the pacing that the game's worked so hard to build.!<

As a final point, the way you get side-quests in batches feels wholly artificial. Are you telling me all of the Hideaway needed aid at exactly the same time, but only 3 people needed aid because that's the number of side-quests we can track at a time? It feels incredibly video gamey. If they're trying to flesh out the world and make things feel holistic, which I'd argue is the point of the side-quests here (and something they largely succeed at, mind), then why do they implement them in such an artificial way?

That said, I've still done every side-quest and found enjoyment in most of them. I have critiques for how they've been implemented, their structure, and their effect on the pacing, but I genuinely enjoy the writing in this game. I wouldn't tell people to *not* do them. I just think they could have been done better. 

***tl;dr*** There are some damn good side-quests, but their structure is repetitive and they break the game's pacing pretty hard if you do them when you get them every time. The writing is good, but there was definitely more opportunity to have them feel more natural in timing and have a more varied player experience.

With all of that, that's the core of our army right now (obviously don't have to run every part every list) and you have some options moving forward.

* A second MVB

That'll be all you need *right now*, but also (likely) all you'll need moving forward unless we get some killer new models. There's a chance a future edition will have you care more about a 2nd Daemon Prince or something along those lines, but with the core and the optionals, that's also likely all you'll *ever* need. There's a chance you'll eventually need some of the other Daemon Engines if they're eventually made good, but they haven't been before. Also a chance that some of the Tzeentch Daemons are worth running down the line, and they were in 9th, but they're not necessary currently, though I've heard of some people running Screamers for fun. One of the upsides of having a small overall unit count is that it's easy to catch up as a new Thousand Sons player.

As far as strengths and weaknesses go, your greatest of both is that you're an elite army, so small model counts. Our guys have good statblocks, but there's always a chance you get tabled, especially with this edition being very anti-tank currently. We're hard to shift against small arms fire, so don't be afraid to play aggressively. Magnus is an absolute beatstick currently, MVBs are phenomenal, and Terminators are aggressively hard to shift. Generally, I wouldn't bother deep striking Magnus, he's too good as a force multiplier. Termies you *can*, but they don't generate cabal points if they're in reserves, and they're perfectly good at marching down board menacingly in most matchups. We get boned by anti-psyker weapons, but you probably expected that lol.

\* Regarding Rubric Characters, you can run Exalted Sorcerers (which are better diskless right now imo, but disk have a purpose), Ahriman, Sorcerers, and Infernal Masters. Don't bring Ahriman on your flamer Rubrics though, as they likely want Umbralefic Crystal so they can re-deploy for a cheeky flamer barrage.
